COUNCIL TAX — Local Government Finance Act 1992 — Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of 
Dwellings) Regulations 1992 — Newbigin (VO) v SJ & J Monk [2017] UKSC 14 — Wilson v Coll 
(LO) [2012] RA 45 — Jackson (VO) v Canary Wharf Limited [2019] UKUT 136 (LC) — Bunyan 
(LO) v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin) — brown water leak into the subject property — ant 
infestation at the subject property — appeal dismissed.

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The panel concluded that the subject property continued to be a hereditament from 20 May 
2025 and therefore its entry should remain in the valuation list. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal relates to a proposal to delete the subject property’s entry from the council tax 
valuation list. 
 
4. 
On 3 July 2025, the Appellant served a proposal on the Respondent Listing Officer. In her 
proposal, the Appellant requested the deletion of the assessment of the subject property from 
the valuation list with effect from 20 May 2025. 
 
5. 
On 14 October 2025, after considering the merits of the proposal, the Respondent Listing 
Officer determined that the proposal was not well founded and a decision notice to that effect 
was issued. 
 
6. 
On 13 January 2026, the Appellant filed an appeal with this Tribunal. 
 
7. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
8. 
The subject property was an end terrace house that entered into the valuation list at band D 
from 19 June 2017 as a new property. It measured 110m2 reduced covered area (RCA) and 
comprised of two bedrooms and two bathrooms.  
 
9. 
In her appeal to the Tribunal, the Appellant contended that the subject property was 
uninhabitable due to serious health and safety risks caused by a brown water leak and a 
subsequent ant infestation. The Appellant advised that, as a result of the safety concerns and 
remedial works, she had to vacate the subject property with her child as she could not safely 
occupy the property. The Appellant confirmed that the works to repair the subject property 
had been conducted between 20 May 2025 and 1 February 2026. 
 
10. Mr Short contended that the subject property remained a hereditament. For a property to no 
longer be a hereditament for the purposes of council tax, it would have to be incapable of 
being repaired to make it suitable for its intended purpose. In this case, he contended that 
the repair works were remedial, rather than structural, in nature. As such, Mr Short argued 
that the repairs were not unreasonable or too extensive to complete. 
 
Relevant Law 
 
11. Part I of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 (the “Act”) makes provision for council tax 
to be payable in respect of domestic hereditaments (“dwellings”) within their administrative 
areas. The term ‘dwelling’ is defined in section 3 of the Act as follows:

3/7 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
3 Meaning of “dwelling” 
 
… 
 
(2) 
Subject to the following provisions of this section, a dwelling is any 
property which— 
 
(a) 
by virtue of the definition of hereditament in section 115(1) of the 
General Rate Act 1967, would have been a hereditament for the 
purposes of that Act if that Act remained in force; and  
 
(b) 
is not for the time being shown or required to be shown in a local 
or a central non-domestic rating list in force at that time; and  
 
(c) 
is not for the time being exempt from local non-domestic rating for 
the purposes of Part III of the Local Government Finance Act 
1988. 
 
12. The definition of dwelling essentially refers back to the definition of a ‘hereditament’ under 
section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 1967, which stated the following:  
 
115 Interpretation  
 
(1) 
In this Act, except where the context otherwise requires, the following 
expressions have the following meanings respectively, that is to say— 
 
… 
 
" hereditament " means property which is or may become liable to 
a rate, being a unit of such property which is, or would fall to be, 
shown as a separate item in the valuation list; 
 
13. If it is determined that a dwelling exists, then the Council Tax (Situation and Valuation of 
Dwellings) Regulations 1992 (SI 1992 No. 550) (the “Valuation Regulations”) requires the 
Listing Officer to make a number of assumptions when valuing a dwelling for entry in the list. 
Relevant to the subject appeal Regulation 6(2)(e) of the Valuation Regulations requires that 
the Listing Officer, and now on appeal, the Tribunal, assumes “that the dwelling was in a 
state of reasonable repair.”  
 
14. The panel must therefore determine whether, considering the physical state of the subject 
property, it remained a dwelling. If it did, the statutory valuation assumptions were engaged.  
 
15. The Respondent Listing Officer relied on and gave reference to the following case law:  
 
• 
Newbigin v Monk [2017] UKSC 14  
• 
Wilson v Coll [2011] EWHC 2824 (Admin)  
• 
Jackson (VO) v Canary Wharf Limited [2019] UKUT 136 (LC) 
• 
Bunyan v Patel [2022] EWHC 1143 (Admin)  
 
Appeal to the Tribunal

16. This appeal was made under regulation 10 of the Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and 
Appeals) (England) Regulations 2009 (SI 2009 No 2270). Relevant to this appeal it provides: 
 
10 Disagreement as to proposed alteration 
 
(1) 
Where the LO has— 
 
(a) 
made a decision under regulation 9(1)(b)(iv); and 
 
(b) 
served a decision notice on the proposer in accordance 
with regulation 9(2), 
 
the proposer or any competent person may appeal to the VTE against the 
LO's decision. 
 
… 
 
Discussion 
 
17. When considering the facts of the case, the panel accepted that repair work was required at 
the subject property to bring it back into use. For council tax purposes, that alone was not 
sufficient for the entry of the subject property to be deleted from the valuation list. For its 
entry to be deleted, the panel must be satisfied that it did not constitute a dwelling. If the 
panel concluded that the dwelling continued to exist, then it must be valued on the statutory 
assumption that it was in reasonable repair, even if in reality it was in need of repair. 
 
18. In determining whether a dwelling exists, the High Court’s judgment in Wilson is relevant. At 
paragraphs 40 and 41, Singh J stated:  
 
“40.  … I accept that as a general matter of law the crucial distinction for the 
purposes of deciding whether there is, or continues to be, a 
hereditament should focus upon whether a property is capable of being 
rendered suitable for occupation (in the present context occupation as a 
dwelling) by undertaking a reasonable amount of repair works. The 
distinction …, in my view, is between a truly derelict property, which is 
incapable of being repaired to make it suitable for its intended purpose, 
and repair which would render it capable again of being occupied for 
the purposes for which it is intended. 
 
“41.  The crucial distinction in that regard is not between repairs which would 
be economic to undertake or uneconomic to undertake.”  
 
19. In Patel, Lang J affirmed the test expounded in Wilson as the correct one to be applied when 
determining whether a hereditament was still in existence (see paragraph [48] of that 
judgment).  
 
20. Thus, in determining whether a hereditament exists, one must consider “having regard to the 
character of the property and a reasonable amount of repair works being undertaken could 
the premises be occupied as a dwelling?” 
 
21. In her proposal to the Respondent Listing Officer, the Appellant detailed the works required to 
bring the property back into use due to the water ingress and the subsequent ant infestation.

The Appellant advised that the property required the removal and replacement of the floors 
and the kitchen to allow for an investigation into the cause of the leak to be carried out. 
Additionally, she advised that she had to vacate the subject property with her young child due 
to health and safety concerns caused by the brown water leak. 
 
22. With the above considerations in mind, the panel turned to the arguments and evidence 
presented on behalf of the Respondent Listing Officer. It was Mr Short’s opinion that the 
subject property was not derelict, with the required repair works being remedial in nature, 
rather than structural. Mr Short argued that no evidence had been provided to suggest that 
the subject property was not a dwelling as at the proposed effective date, or from any other 
date, and it had therefore not ceased to be a dwelling for council tax purposes. 
 
23. After considering the submissions made on behalf of the Respondent Listing Officer, the 
panel turned to the evidence and arguments presented by the Appellant. In the bundle, the 
Appellant provided fifteen photographs taken between May 2025 and January 2026 of the 
work carried out at the subject property. Upon reviewing the photographs, the panel found 
that the majority of the works conducted were carried out on the ground floor of the subject 
property and the ensuite bathroom but did not impact the property in its entirety. Additionally, 
based on the photographs, the panel noted that there was evidence that the subject property 
did not have what could be considered as a functional kitchen while investigative works were 
carried out, however, the connection points remained in place to allow for installation. 
Therefore, the panel determined that the evidence provided was not sufficient to demonstrate 
that the subject property could not be utilised as a dwelling with reasonable repair. 
 
24. In addition to the photographs, the panel was provided with a copy of a Quality Surveyor’s 
report completed by PBA Planning following a visit to the subject property on 3 June 2025. 
The panel found that the report concluded that the soil pipe serving the main bathroom had 
been leaking since the subject property was first occupied and that the extensive ant 
infestation at the property had been caused by the leak. One of the recommendations arising 
from the report was that the Appellant should vacate the subject property. However, upon 
reviewing the document, the panel found that the inspection was focused solely on the 
kitchen area, rather than the subject property as a whole. Consequently, the panel found the 
report was limited in scope and did not provide a comprehensive assessment of the overall 
condition or habitability of the property. While the report identified defects and recommended 
temporary vacation of the property, the panel noted that it did not conclude that the dwelling 
was incapable of repair within its character or that there were structural concerns as a result 
of the brown water leak.  
 
25. The final piece of evidence provided to the panel by the Appellant was an ant control report 
prepared by PGH Pest Prevention in 2025. The panel found that the report identified nine ant 
nests within the kitchen area and a further nest in the ensuite bathroom. The panel noted that 
the report also suggested that the infestation was likely linked to a long-standing leak from 
the soil pipe, which had created conditions conducive to ant activity. Whilst the panel 
acknowledged that the infestation and associated damage required extensive investigative, 
remedial and pest control works, it found that the report was primarily concerned with 
identifying the source of the infestation and recommending measures to eradicate it. The 
panel determined that the recommended works were directed towards the investigation, 
treatment and repair of defects that were capable of being remedied, and the report did not 
conclude that the subject property was beyond repair, structurally unsound, or truly derelict.  
 
26. In reviewing the evidence, the panel turned to the principles established in Newbigin v Monk 
and Jackson v Canary Wharf. Although these cases concerned non-domestic rating, the

panel considered them relevant in assisting with the determination of whether a hereditament 
continued to exist. The case law established that a property could cease to be a 
hereditament where it was undergoing a scheme of reconstruction or redevelopment that 
rendered it incapable of beneficial occupation whilst in a transitional state. However, having 
considered the Appellant’s evidence and the nature of the works undertaken, the panel found 
that the subject property had been undergoing remedial repair and reinstatement works 
arising from a leaking soil pipe and ant infestation, rather than a programme of 
reconstruction, redevelopment, or structural alteration. The works were intended to restore 
the property to its previous condition and did not alter its use, layout, character, or identity as 
a dwelling. Furthermore, during the hearing, the panel found that the duration of the works 
had been significantly influenced by the investigation and processing of the home warranty 
claim, rather than by the scale or complexity of the physical works themselves. Therefore, the 
principles of Newbigin v Monk and Jackson v Canary Wharf did not apply to this case. 
 
27. Having regard to the above conclusions, the panel found that the subject property could not 
be regarded as a truly derelict property that was incapable of occupation for its intended use 
with a reasonable amount of repair; this was supported by the fact that the property had been 
repaired by the time that the appeal had been initiated. The subject property was therefore a 
hereditament (a dwelling) and the statutory assumption of reasonable state of repair had to 
be applied in the valuation. 
 
Conclusion 
 
28. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel was satisfied that the subject 
property remained a dwelling. Therefore, its entry should remain in the valuation list. 
 
29. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed.  
 
Right of further appeal 
 
30. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
31. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.
